reference.answer: Market capitalization, or Market Cap, is calculated by multiplying the share price by the number of shares. It represents the current market perception of the company's worth. On the other hand, NAV, or net asset value, is the value of the company's stock divided by the number of shares, also known as the book value. NAV reflects the value of the company's assets if it were to sell everything, pay off its debts, and shut down. While Market Cap represents current market sentiment and future expectations, NAV provides a measure of the company's tangible asset value per share. These two values often differ significantly, especially for companies expected to grow or those with substantial intangible assets. NAV is a measurable value, derived from known factors, while Market Cap is determined by the stock price, which is influenced not only by NAV but also by future expectations.

Absolutely. There are probably special cases where this could cause problems, however; any case where A's purchase of B's stock (or vice versa) runs afoul of regulation would be one such case. For example, if company A wants to own a controlling interest in company B and appoint members of its board of directors and both companies were in the same heavily-concentrated market, regulators may frown on the potential for decreased competition. Such regulations may apply to any purchase of a controlling interest in a company, though.

If you do your research properly and buy into stable companies you shouldn't need to bother about temporary market movements or crashes (do pay attention to deterioration on the businesses you own though). When buying stocks you should be aiming for the very long run. As mentioned by Victor, do your research, I recommend you start it by looking into 'value stocks' should you choose that path.

As your company grows, you tend to add people in "layers." The top layer is the first founder or founder. There may be one, two, three, or more of you, but you all start working at about the same time, and you all take the same risk: quitting your jobs to work for a new and unproven company. 
The second layer is the first actual employees. By the time you hire this layer, you've got cash coming in from somewhere (investors or customers—doesn't matter). These people didn't take as much risk because they got a salary from day one, and honestly, they didn't start the company, they joined it as a job. The third layer consists of later employees. By the time they joined the company, it was going pretty well. Each "layer" will be approximately one year for many companies. When your company is big enough to sell to Google or go public, you probably have about six layers: the founders and roughly five layers of employees. Each successive layer is more significant. It's very important to keep your employees happy and ensure they feel part of something other than a job. Make them feel like they're part of a family and support system.

rag_history_before_turn.content: What's the difference between Market Cap and NAV?

Market capitalization, or Market Cap, is calculated by multiplying the share price by the number of shares. It represents the current market perception of the company's worth. On the other hand, NAV, or net asset value, is the value of the company's stock divided by the number of shares, also known as the book value. NAV reflects the value of the company's assets if it were to sell everything, pay off its debts, and shut down. While Market Cap represents current market sentiment and future expectations, NAV provides a measure of the company's tangible asset value per share. These two values often differ significantly, especially for companies expected to grow or those with substantial intangible assets. NAV is a measurable value, derived from known factors, while Market Cap is determined by the stock price, which is influenced not only by NAV but also by future expectations.

Unless you want to spend all your time looking up money stuff, the adviser is going to have a better grasp of ""money stuff"" then you, because they do spend all their time doing it. reference.answer: A financial advisor is a professional service provider who can handle tasks that you either don't have time for or prefer someone else to manage. If you lack the time or interest to manage your investments, hiring a financial advisor is a good idea. It's generally better to work with an advisor who charges an annual fee based on a percentage of your account value rather than one who gets paid based on transactions. Advisors compensated in the latter way may have a vested interest in making frequent changes to your account, which might not be in your best interest. It's important to be cautious of advisors who promote expensive mutual funds with sales loads or annuities. Additionally, your advisor's compensation structure should be transparent.
